Here is my paint scheme on my Dust Tactics Allies Ranger squads. It is a rather simple paint scheme, but I like it. I decided on a the lighter Khaki color for the long coats as the darker brown though more realistic to what US troops had didn't make them look very American, and greens made them look less World War II.

I am not happy with the trousers. I think they are too green. I have since picked up some Vallejo US Field Drab. I just have too much on the needs to be painted pile before I can go back an change up the color on stuff that is more or less complete.

If anyone cares about the paint colors I used, here they are:

Helmets, Body Armor = Vallejo Brown Violet

Longcoat = Game Color Khaki

Gaiters = Game Color Khaki (I just didn't dry brush the color back up)

Trousers, Base = Vallejo Reflective Green (I suggest using US Dark Green instead for the pants)

Boots, Gloves = Vallejo Chocolate Brown

Metal parts of weapons = Black with light dry brush of Gun Metal Blue

Wood parts of weapons = Vallejo Red Leather mixed with a little Chocolate Brown

Skin = various shades of flesh colors or Chocolate Brown (I like variation in skin tones)

Gonna make a post that lists some common (free) bioinformatics tools since it always crops up.

Quality Control

FastQC

PreqC

Sequence Pre-processing

FastUniq - Removes PCR duplicates

Skewer - Removes PCR adaptors

Musket - Error correction

There are a host of programs for static cuts, google is your friend for these.

Sequence Assembly;

de novo

When I say 'data format' below I am referring to the raw Fastq read stats like; base pair length, paired end data, paired end overlap, etc.

Discovar - de Bruijn graph based assembly. Very easy to run. Heavy RAM usage, moderate CPU and disk space. Requires a specific data format.

Meraculous - de Bruijn graph based assembly. Uses a ton of disk space, but not that much RAM, average CPU. Takes most data formats.

SOAP - de Bruijn graph based assembly. Tries to balance out RAM/CPU/disk space usage, takes a bit longer to run. Takes most data formats.

SGA - Takes a very long time, but accepts most data.

Abyss - de Bruijn graph based assembly. RAM skew over CPU and disk space. Takes most data formats

Reference based

BWA

Bowtie

Sequence Alignment

BLAST

Clustal

Visualization

UCSC Genome Browser

Ensemble Genome Browser

And now we have a very basic list! Feel free to add to it/comment on it.

More molecular structure tools

VMD NAMD

Linux Distro (since it's free)

Bio-Linux

The #1 important tool these days is R and bioconductor.

Why? Because literate programming with R Markdown (usually in the RStudio context) is the way to go. It is never enough to just run your analysis, you must also document it and you must run it reproducibly.

 

To find other tools I go to the curated, searchable links directory at bioinformatics.ca.

 

Jalview, the multiple sequence alignment editor, is incredibly useful to organize data and annotations.

 

Nb., because I see it listed here: do not use Clustal! Ever. As many studies have shown, Clustal is outdated and inferior to practically all other MSA tools (except for the most trivial cases). A good source for MSA tools is at the EBI.
